title: Do not trust the first AI answer
hook: AI is useful, but the first answer is usually a draft.
tip: Ask for the answer, then ask the model to check what could be wrong, missing, or risky before you use it.
why: That second pass catches weak logic, missing context, and confident mistakes.
steps: Give the model the real task.
Ask it to review its own answer.
prompt: Review your answer. What might be wrong, missing, unclear, or risky? Then give me a corrected version.
question: What task would you always review before using an AI answer?

title: Context beats clever prompts
hook: A simple prompt with good context beats a fancy prompt with no background.
tip: Before asking ChatGPT for help, give it the audience, current situation, constraints, and what a good answer should look like.
why: ChatGPT responds better when it understands the real problem and who the answer is for.
steps: Say what you are working on.
prompt: I am working on [task] for [audience]. The situation is [context]. I must follow [constraints]. A good result should [outcome].
question: Which piece of context improves your prompts the most?

title: Tell ChatGPT the format first
hook: You can save time by describing the answer you want before ChatGPT starts writing.
tip: Ask for the exact length, structure, tone, and format. You will spend less time trimming and rearranging the result.
why: A clear output format reduces unnecessary words and makes the first draft easier to use.
steps: Ask for only the final answer.
prompt: Answer in five bullets. Use plain language. Keep each bullet under 20 words. Give me only the final answer.
question: What output format do you ask AI for most often?

title: Use screenshots when words are slow
hook: Sometimes showing the problem is faster than explaining it.
tip: Share a screenshot with sensitive details removed, point to the issue, and ask the model to explain what it sees before suggesting steps.
why: Images give the model useful visual context and reduce misunderstandings.
prompt: Describe what you see in this screenshot. Do not guess hidden details. Then give me the safest next three steps.
question: What visual task would be easier to show AI than explain?

title: Automate the repeat work first
hook: The best first automation is usually not the flashy one.
tip: Start with a task your team repeats every week, such as status updates, inbox sorting, report drafts, or document cleanup.
why: Small repeatable wins build trust faster than one large, risky automation project.
prompt: Turn this repeated task into a checklist. Mark what AI can draft, what needs a human decision, and what proof should be saved.
question: Which weekly task would you automate first?

title: Turn long documents into decisions
hook: Use Claude like a careful reader, not a magic answer machine.
tip: Ask Claude to separate facts, decisions, risks, open questions, and follow-up actions from a long document.
why: A structured review makes a long document easier to check without replacing your judgment.
prompt: Read this document and return five sections: facts, decisions, risks, open questions, and next actions. Cite the relevant section for each point.
question: What is the longest document you regularly need to review?

title: Make Claude create the handoff
hook: A good AI session should leave the next person with something usable.
tip: At the end of a task, ask Claude to create a short handoff with decisions, files changed, checks completed, risks, and the next action.
why: A consistent handoff makes AI-assisted work easier to continue and audit.
prompt: Create a handoff with: objective, decisions, work completed, files affected, checks run, known risks, and next action.
question: What information is usually missing from your project handoffs?

title: Ask AI for three email versions
hook: One AI draft can trap you in one tone.
tip: Ask for three versions: direct, warm, and concise. Compare them, then combine the strongest parts in your own voice.
why: Options make it easier to choose the right tone without accepting the first draft.
prompt: Write three versions of this email: direct, warm, and concise. Keep the facts unchanged and avoid corporate jargon.
question: Which email tone is hardest for you to get right?

title: Test models with your real work
hook: A model leaderboard cannot tell you which model fits your workflow.
tip: Give two models the same real task, context, and scoring checklist. Compare accuracy, usefulness, speed, and the amount of correction required.
why: Your own repeatable test reveals more than a general benchmark.
prompt: Score this output from 1 to 5 for accuracy, completeness, clarity, and effort to correct. Explain each score with evidence.
question: Which real task would you use to compare two AI models?

title: Do not switch models for hype
hook: A new AI model matters only if it improves work you actually do.
tip: When a model launches, check its official capabilities, limits, price, privacy terms, and performance on one task you already understand.
why: A small evaluation prevents expensive tool switching based on launch-day excitement.
prompt: Build a comparison table for this model: capabilities, limits, price, privacy, best use cases, and evidence still needed.
question: What must a new model improve before you switch?

title: Structure complex Claude prompts
hook: Long prompts work better when instructions and source material are clearly separated.
tip: Label the task, context, constraints, source material, and required output in distinct sections.
why: Clear boundaries help Claude follow complex instructions without mixing your source material with the task.
prompt:
TASK: [goal]
CONTEXT: [background]
CONSTRAINTS: [rules]
SOURCE: [material]
OUTPUT: [required structure]
question: Which part of your longer prompts becomes unclear most often?

title: Build a reusable context pack
hook: Do not make the model rediscover your business every time.
tip: Keep a reviewed context pack with your goals, terminology, policies, examples, and current constraints. Update it when the business changes.
why: Stable context improves consistency and reduces repeated prompting.
prompt: Use only this context pack for company-specific facts. Flag anything the pack does not answer instead of guessing.
question: What information would belong in your reusable context pack?

title: Set boundaries before giving AI tools
hook: An AI agent becomes riskier when it can click, send, delete, or publish.
tip: Define what the agent may read, draft, change, and submit. Require approval for irreversible or public actions.
why: Clear boundaries preserve speed while preventing one bad decision from becoming a real-world mistake.
prompt: Create an action policy with allowed actions, blocked actions, approval points, required proof, and failure handling.
question: Which action should your AI agent never take without approval?

title: Keep proof before you scale AI
hook: If an AI workflow matters, keep proof of what it did.
tip: Save inputs, outputs, decisions, screenshots, and approvals for important automated work.
why: Proof makes automation safer because you can understand what happened when something goes wrong.
prompt: Design a proof checklist for this workflow. Include input, output, decision, approver, timestamp, and recovery action.
question: What proof would you need before trusting an automated workflow?

title: Your AI moat is the workflow
hook: Access to the same AI model is not a lasting business advantage.
tip: A stronger moat comes from trusted context, a useful workflow, customer insight, human judgment, and feedback that improves the system over time.
why: Competitors can buy the same model, but they cannot instantly copy how your team learns and delivers value.
prompt: Assess our AI moat across five areas: proprietary context, workflow integration, customer access, feedback loops, and switching costs.
question: What part of your workflow would be hardest for a competitor to copy?

title: Data alone is not an AI moat
hook: Having data is useful. Turning it into a trusted advantage is harder.
tip: The real value comes from clean permissioned data, domain knowledge, workflow placement, measurable outcomes, and a feedback loop.
why: Unorganized data without trust, access rules, or a useful decision point rarely creates durable value.
prompt: Evaluate this dataset as an AI advantage. Check permission, uniqueness, quality, workflow relevance, measurable value, and feedback.
question: Where does your data become useful inside a real decision?

title: Know what not to build
hook: Not every AI feature should become an internal software project.
tip: Buy common capabilities, build where your workflow is genuinely distinctive, and partner where expertise or risk is too expensive to recreate.
why: The right boundary protects time and keeps investment focused on what customers actually value.
prompt: Recommend buy, build, or partner for this AI capability. Compare differentiation, cost, speed, data sensitivity, maintenance, and risk.
question: Which part of your AI workflow is truly unique enough to build?

title: Measure correction time too
hook: A fast AI draft is not a saving if someone spends longer fixing it.
tip: Measure total task time, correction time, error rate, and outcome quality before calling an AI workflow successful.
why: Real return comes from better completed work, not impressive generation speed.
prompt: Create a simple AI value scorecard using total time, correction time, error rate, output quality, and business outcome.
question: Which AI task saves generation time but still costs too much review time?
